newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa gold mines reform a risky business.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa gold mines reform a risky business.

text.p: Amid the ferocious din of drill bits a group of young black men crouch deep in the bowels of the earth working in one of the world's most dangerous industries -- South African gold mining.

They labour in a hot and dark gallery just one meter (three feet) high with 1.6 km (a mile) of solid rock above their heads. A slight earth tremor could bring the roof down, turning their workplace into a tomb.
It used to be said that it cost a miner's life for every ton of South African gold mined. That is no longer exactly true.
The last available safety data for the gold mining industry showed that 411 men died in 1995, up from 357 in 1994, while the industry produced 522 tons of gold, down from 583 in 1994.
"It is a very hostile environment," said Llewellyn Kriel, spokesman for the Chamber of Mines.

The death rate in 1995 per 1,000 miners was 1.23, up from 1.03 the previous year. The 1995 figures were skewed by the horrific Vaal Reefs disaster in which 104 men perished when a runaway train plunged down a shaft, crushing an elevator.
Nonetheless, the last decade has seen the fatality rate follow a shallow downward trend along with the reportable injury rate. In 1985 the injury rate was at 27.49, while in 1995 it stood at 18.53.
Industry experts say the sector is sharpening up its act and making real progress in improving its record. "Little by little we are winning the race," Kriel said.
The reasons for the changes are many.
Mining wealth was the backbone of the riches that built South Africa. Using poorly paid, uneducated and unskilled workers the mines reaped huge profits from beneath the soil.

However, as South Africa's apartheid system began to crumble changes became necessary. The process has speeded up since the African National Congress won the country's first all-race elections in 1994.

The new Mining Health and Safety Act came into effect in January this year, with a wide range of reforms. It gave a legislative base to health and safety committees involving unions and gave miners the right to refuse to do dangerous work.
South Africa's largest mine union, the National Union of Mineworkers, is optimistic about the prospects for the act's effectiveness.

"The NUM sees that there is more to be done on health and safety...(but) we are certain that if these committees go forward in the right way then health and safety will improve," said Welcome Mboniso, NUM mine health and safety co-ordinator.
Wages have also improved. Bonus plans have been introduced, earning miners more cash and lifting productivity.
St. Helena Mines Ltd. manager Joe Hardy said a new bonus plan at his mine had seen productivity soar and extended its lifespan by at least 11 years.
"Without more flexible bonuses there was no incentive for them (the miners)," Hardy said.
Education of workers has improved as mines instituted adult education programmes and set up training colleges.

This has seen the rise of English usage on the mines and the decline of Fanakalo, a tongue developed from English, Afrikaans and African languages purely as a crude means of instruction for ethnically mixed miners.
"You can now communicate with your workers in English and explain why they are doing things rather than just shoving orders down their throats," Kriel said.

Analysts say the changing nature of mining is not due to any philanthropic conversion away from the bad habits of the past. In order to survive in the new South Africa, mines have to adjust to the political realities of majority rule.

"It is clearly now in their (the mines') interest to cater to representatives of government and unions otherwise they can make things very tough for the mines," said Angus Auchterlonie, analyst at stockbroker Mathison and Hollidge Inc.
Despite the advances South African mining will always be a dangerous business. South African mines are deeper than any others and deep mining is dangerous mining.
The rocks are under greater stress, temperatures are hotter and it takes longer to get to a blasting face or accident site.

The country's ageing gold mines are also heading further into the ground, in search of the diminishing ore supplies. Anglo American Corp. of South Africa Ltd already plans to sink mines up to five km (three miles) deep.
